A spatiotemporal difference-enhancement network with semantic flow alignment for fine-grained cropland change detection
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Accurate cropland change detection from high-resolution remote sensing images is essential for agricultural resource monitoring, land management, and food security. Existing methods struggle with two primary challenges: (1) severe pseudo-change noise and false alarms, caused by sole reliance on simple spatial or temporal difference enhancement, and (2) inadequate fine-grained cropland change detection, resulting from boundary detail degradation during fixed interpolation decoding. To address these issues, we propose a S patio T emporal D ifference- E nhancement N etwork (STDENet) with semantic flow alignment for effective cropland change detection from high-resolution remote sensing images. Built on a pyramid vision transformer V2 (PVT-V2) encoder, STDENet integrates three key innovations: a spatiotemporal dual-branch difference enhancement (STDDE) module that jointly captures temporal variations and spatial discrepancies to suppress irrelevant responses from unchanged or spectrally similar regions; an adaptive boundary-aware (ABA) module that dynamically extracts four-directional texture cues to enhance boundary representations; and a semantic flow-aligned decoding (SFAD) module that predicts semantic flow fields to warp high-level difference features and align them with low-level spatial details for fine-grained structure recovery. We evaluate the STDENet on one self-constructed dataset, DYCD, and two public benchmark datasets, CLCD and Hi-CNA. Comparative experiments confirm that STDENet consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on all three datasets, improving IoU by 3.41 %, 4.90 %, and 1.98 % over the second-best methods on DYCD, CLCD, and Hi-CNA, respectively. By enhancing global structural information through the spatial branch and local change responses through the temporal branch, the spatiotemporal interaction design improves the feature separability of cropland changes. Semantic flow alignment helps restore fine-grained details by producing a more stable decoding process for local contours in cropland change patches. STDENet also demonstrates stronger resistance to interference and better adaptability to phenological variations among crop growth, pre-sowing, and post-harvest periods. Large-scale applications further indicate its generalization ability across heterogeneous cropland structures.

title: A multi-source remote sensing benchmark for event-level wildfire spread prediction in California using spatiotemporal deep learning
abstract: Satellite-based wildfire spread studies differ in data organization and evaluation procedures, making model performance difficult to compare. We constructed an event-level benchmark to compare model performance and examine how the models used the available inputs. The benchmark covers California during 2012 to 2021 and combines VIIRS 375 m active-fire observations, MODIS NDVI-derived vegetation information, and ERA5-Land wind fields. Each wildfire event was represented on a fixed 100 × 100 grid. Each sequence sample used ten historical daily steps to predict the next-day satellite-observed fire-state mask. Six spatiotemporal models (CNN-LSTM, Vision Transformer, ConvLSTM, Pairwise-ConvLSTM, Patchwise-ConvLSTM, and ST-GNN) were evaluated using common input definitions, preprocessing procedures, prediction targets, and metrics. Integrated Gradients was applied after training to quantify attributions from the five raster input channels to the next-day model outputs. Pairwise-ConvLSTM achieved the lowest overall RMSE of 0.0495 on the cumulative wildfire dataset. Among the five evaluated Patchwise-ConvLSTM configurations, the 7 × 7 setting achieved the highest observed F1-score (0.955), with precision (0.962) and recall (0.949). On the newly burned-pixel subset, the same configuration achieved precision (0.916), recall (0.888), and F1-score (0.902). The attribution analysis showed larger mean absolute values for vegetation-constrained unburned states (7.23 × 10−5) and prior cumulative fire history (5.13 × 10−5) than for newly detected fire pixels (1.81 × 10−5), the eastward wind component (7.01 × 10−6), and the northward wind component (8.97 × 10−6). The benchmark provides a common framework for assessing predictive performance and model input use in next-day satellite-observed wildfire spread prediction.

title: Vegetation restoration enhances drought resilience through threshold-dependent carbon–water regulation in a semi-arid sandy ecosystem
abstract: Drought increasingly constrains ecosystem functioning in semi-arid regions, yet the nonlinear thresholds through which vegetation restoration regulates carbon–water processes and ecosystem resilience remain poorly understood. In this study, a drought–carbon–water–resilience framework was developed to assess how vegetation restoration affects ecosystem drought resilience in the Mu Us Sandy Land, a representative semi-arid sandy ecosystem in northern China. MODIS products, including MOD17A2H/MOD17A3H for gross and net primary productivity (GPP and NPP), MOD16A2 for evapotranspiration (ET), MOD13A2 for the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), MOD11A2 for land surface temperature (LST), and MOD44B for vegetation cover, were used for the period 2001–2020 and harmonized to a 1000-m spatial resolution and an annual temporal scale to quantify water use efficiency (WUE), carbon use efficiency (CUE), the temperature–vegetation drought index (TVDI), ecosystem resistance, recovery, resilience, and a restoration intensity index (RII). The results showed that drought intensity increased slightly over time, while WUE and CUE exhibited contrasting spatial patterns and different sensitivities to drought. At the pixel scale, temporal correlations between annual TVDI and WUE/CUE were positive over 83.74% and 69.78% of the study area, respectively, indicating that carbon–water use efficiency often showed compensatory increases under mild-to-moderate drought conditions. In contrast, the regional drought-gradient analysis revealed threshold-dependent responses of WUE and CUE to increasing TVDI, with critical thresholds at approximately TVDI = 0.67 and TVDI = 0.66, respectively; beyond these thresholds, both water and carbon use efficiency declined rapidly. Strong restoration areas showed higher RSwue and RScue than weak/no restoration and degradation areas, and the proportion of high-resilience areas increased with restoration intensity, particularly for CUE-based resilience. Hierarchical regression further showed that RII provided additional explanatory power for ecosystem resilience after controlling for drought intensity, although its effects differed between water-use and carbon-use processes. These findings indicate that vegetation restoration enhances drought resilience through threshold-dependent carbon–water regulation, but its effectiveness depends on vegetation structure and water availability. Threshold-based monitoring and structure-optimized restoration should therefore be prioritized in semi-arid sandy ecosystem management.

title: The salinity-aridity nexus modulates eco-hydrological impacts of vegetation enhancement and desertification across saline-alkali drylands in northern China
abstract: Vegetation dynamics in drylands fundamentally restructure the land-atmosphere interface, yet the resulting surface water-energy coupling across saline-alkali environments remains insufficiently understood due to the complex interplay between climatic aridity and edaphic salinity. By integrating multi-decadal satellite observations with a biogeophysical decomposition framework, we quantified the growing-season impacts of vegetation enhancement (cropland expansion and grassland restoration) alongside desertification across the saline-alkali drylands of northern China from 2003 to 2020. Our results demonstrated that vegetation enhancement induced significant localized surface cooling, peaking in barren-to-cropland conversions (−0.674 ± 0.02 K), followed by grassland-to-cropland conversions (−0.066 ± 0.007 K) and barren-to-grassland restoration (−0.017 ± 0.009 K), whereas desertification exhibited a subtle warming tendency (+0.005 ± 0.0003 K). These thermal responses were primarily governed by non-radiative, evapotranspiration-mediated processes. Furthermore, the salinity-aridity nexus modulated regional energy partitioning through two divergent hydro-edaphic pathways. In reclaimed irrigated cropland, management interventions alleviated ambient matric and osmotic constraints, while intensifying regional water consumption. In contrast, non-irrigated restored grasslands exhibited a functional decoupling between canopy greening and evaporative cooling, reflecting conservative stomatal regulation enforced by compound soil matric and osmotic stresses. The marginal warming accompanying desertification indicated an impaired surface evaporative buffer following vegetation loss and secondary salinization. By elucidating how the salinity-aridity nexus modulates land-surface water-energy coupling, these findings highlight the necessity to align restoration strategies with local hydro-edaphic capacities, balancing the microclimatic cooling of irrigated agriculture against the long-term hydrological sustainability of natural grasslands under accelerating global change.

title: TMSC: A tri-regional mask-guided semantic calibration framework for zero-shot anomaly detection
Remote sensing reveals vegetation-specific structure–function controls on carbon sequestration services in phenologically heterogeneous alpine ecosystems
Beyond spectral diversity: Spectral detection of dominant species decodes grassland plant diversity across management regimes
PACE hyperspectral observations enable a new paradigm for global mapping of terrestrial gross primary production
abstract: Accurate quantification of terrestrial gross primary production (GPP) is fundamental to understanding plant productivity, ecosystem function, and carbon-climate feedbacks. Existing approaches typically rely on meteorological, soil, and other ancillary inputs, which introduce substantial uncertainties at regional to global scales. NASA's Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission, carrying the Ocean Color Instrument (OCI), provides the first contiguous global hyperspectral observations from space. Using 122 spectral bands from PACE, we developed a data-driven framework based on partial least squares regression to generate an 8-day global GPP product. The model achieves a robust performance (R 2 = 0.71, RMSE = 1.93 gC m −2 d −1 ), comparable to models that incorporate meteorological drivers, and outperforms approaches based on broadband reflectance or vegetation indices. PACE-derived GPP showed broad spatial correspondence with solar-induced fluorescence (SIF), including hotspots across high productivity regions such as the U.S. Corn Belt, the Amazon and Congo basins, and the Indo-Gangetic and North China Plains. This strong spatial coherence supports the physiological relevance of the PACE retrievals. Our results demonstrate that hyperspectral observations provide a direct, observation-driven framework for estimating plant productivity at the global scale, opening new opportunities for monitoring vegetation responses to environmental change.

title: Assessing the detectability of standing dead trees in PlanetScope imagery
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Standing dead trees (SDTs) play a critical role in forest biodiversity assessment, disturbance monitoring, and carbon cycling. High-resolution optical satellite imagery offers an opportunity for large-scale SDT detection by providing finer spatial detail than moderate-resolution sensors. Despite this advantage, isolated SDTs may occupy only part of a PlanetScope pixel, allowing their signals to mix with those of live canopy, non-woody vegetation, and shadows. As a result, it is necessary to quantify signal detectability and detection stability across these conditions. To address this issue, this study uses PlanetScope imagery at 3 m resolution and Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV)-derived reference annotations to develop a multi-level, response-based SDT framework for analyzing SDT detectability from the aspect of the segmentation models, SDT density, and SDT patch sizes. UAV annotations are first aggregated to the PlanetScope pixel scale to generate hard labels and soft labels. The deep and machine learning models are then trained to select a stable reference semantic model and assess the consistency of SDT detection responses across architectures. All deep learning segmentation models produced consistent detectability responses, with HRNet achieving the best performance, with a binary F1 of 0.86. A single-pixel SDT signal became evident mainly when SDT cover proportion reached the 70 %-80 %, whereas neighborhood support lowered this change to a local SDT density of 20 %–30 %. Patch-level analysis indicated more stable detection for SDT patches larger than 90–180 m 2 . Furthermore, reliable PlanetScope detection is associated with SDT dominance, spatial aggregation, and high local SDT density . The proposed framework provides a detectability analysis approach for evaluating the stability of SDT detection in 3 m satellite imagery and the consistency of these responses across semantic segmentation models, linking high-resolution satellite imagery probability mapping with ultra-high-resolution UAV-based observations.

title: Satellite remote sensing of polar clouds: a review of cloud detection, phase identification, and microphysical property retrieval (2001–2025)
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Polar clouds play important roles in regulating the surface energy budget, atmospheric moisture cycle, precipitation, and sea-ice variability, while their occurrence, vertical structure, thermodynamic phase, and microphysical properties remain difficult to characterize consistently across the Arctic and Antarctic. Satellite remote sensing enables broad-scale monitoring of polar clouds, yet high-albedo snow and ice surfaces, weak cloud–surface thermal contrast, frequent temperature inversions, and persistent mixed-phase conditions make cloud detection and property retrieval substantially more difficult than at lower latitudes. This review synthesizes progress during the quarter-century 2001–2025 in polar cloud satellite remote sensing with a focus on satellite-based polar cloud detection, cloud phase identification, and microphysical retrieval. It first analyzes the synergistic monitoring capabilities of multi-source satellite sensors, including passive multispectral imagers, active radars and lidars, and microwave radiometers. It then explores in depth the evolution of cloud detection methods from static physical thresholds to deep learning algorithms that integrate spatial information and multimodal features. For cloud phase identification and microphysical retrieval, this paper reviews the physical principles and technical limitations of representative methods, including threshold and Lookup Table (LUT) methods, Optimal Estimation Method (OEM), variational and Bayesian retrievals, analytical and empirical methods, and machine-learning approaches, with particular attention to the challenges associated with ice–liquid phase partitioning and vertical heterogeneity in polar mixed-phase clouds. Finally, it identifies the deficiencies in current research regarding the application of far-infrared and high-frequency submillimeter-wave bands, the construction of full-spatiotemporal coverage observation networks, and the physical consistency of data-driven models, and outlines priorities for developing a continuous, multi-dimensional polar cloud monitoring system based on coordinated high- and low-orbit observations, recent and forthcoming satellite instruments, and physically constrained artificial intelligence.

title: OESTR: An orbit-encoding spatiotemporal reconstruction framework for joint daytime–nighttime FY-3D LST gap filling
Uncertainty as the key to interoperability: Traceable frameworks for space-based imaging spectroscopy
abstract: By the end of this decade, several space agencies and commercial operators will develop and launch the next generation of space-based Earth observation satellites. This paper focuses on imaging spectroradiometers, which measure solar radiation reflected by the Earth’s surface across the ultra-violet, visible and short-wave infrared spectral ranges using hyperspectral sensors. To enable interoperable use of datasets from this growing constellation of sensors, it is essential to understand and manage differences between the measurements of the same target under similar conditions. These differences arise from multiple factors: real variations due to instrument design (e.g., differing spectral responses or viewing geometries), differences in Level 1 processing approaches based on pre-flight and post-launch calibration strategies, differences in higher-level processing into biophysical quantities, and any residual biases between sensors caused by measurement or processing errors — some of which may not be fully captured in reported uncertainties. A consistent approach to the analysis and documentation of uncertainties supports intercomparison between datasets. By assessing whether measurements agree within the expected uncertainty associated with the comparison, or identifying and quantifying systematic deviations when they do not, it becomes possible to validate interoperability and diagnose discrepancies. This paper outlines key concepts for harmonising uncertainty analysis and reporting techniques across missions, including the use of structured uncertainty propagation frameworks such as uncertainty trees. The goal is to initiate a roadmap for understanding and quantifying uncertainties in a way that facilitates robust intercomparison of multiple space-based imaging spectroradiometer measurements.

title: Multi-temporal dual-frequency bistatic InSAR reveals effective scattering-height dynamics of temperate forest structural phenology

title: Revealing the influence of volcanic plumes on lake water quality parameters derived using remote sensing methods
abstract: Satellite-derived observations of inland waters are widely used in environmental monitoring and climate research, often forming the basis of long-term analyses in the absence of continuous in situ measurements. However, the influence of transient atmospheric phenomena, such as volcanic plumes, on these datasets remains insufficiently quantified. In this study, we investigate the extent to which volcanic plumes influence lake surface water temperature (LSWT), turbidity, and chlorophyll-a measurements derived from ESA Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Lakes. Using a multi-sensor approach, we leverage MISR and MODIS observations to analyse plume–lake interactions during the 2011–2012 eruption of Puyehue-Cordón Caulle (PCC), Chile. Results indicate that while standard cloud screening procedures remove a substantial proportion of plume-affected observations, residual impacts remain. Notably, lake observations are influenced not only when plumes directly overlay the lake surface but also when plumes are proximal but not visually detectable over the lake, indicating the influence of diffuse aerosol particles. Analysis of aerosol microphysical properties demonstrates that particle-based classification can achieve approximately 67% accuracy, in identifying plume-affected observations but is limited by temporal variability in volcanic plume composition. In contrast, proximity-based approaches more consistently capture plume influence, suggesting that spatial context is critical for effective data flagging. These findings highlight a previously under-recognised source of uncertainty in satellite-derived inland water quality datasets. They support the implementation of proximity-based quality flags to improve data reliability in regions affected by volcanic activity in situations where consistent particle-based observations are unavailable.

title: A transferable satellite-derived bathymetry model without site-specific calibration for Case-1 optically shallow waters using Sentinel-2/MSI imagery
abstract: Accurate bathymetry in optically shallow waters (OSWs), particularly across coral reef environments, is essential for coastal ecosystem management and benthic habitat monitoring. Satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) offers a scalable alternative, but reliance on in situ depth measurements constrains its application in data-sparse OSW regions, while the coupling between water-column and benthic signals limits retrieval accuracy. Here, we developed OSW-SDB, a simulation-based SDB model for Case-1 OSWs that is not tailored to a specific region and accounts for variations in benthic reflectance. Using a newly developed benthic reflectance library comprising 2,100 spectra, we generated 200,000 pairs of water depth and remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) by radiative transfer simulations spanning diverse water-column optical properties and benthic reflectance conditions. An XGBoost model was trained based on the simulated dataset using SHAP-selected multispectral features, with 6,711 matched ICESat-2/ATL24 observations additionally used for hyperparameter optimization. OSW-SDB achieved coefficient of determination (R2) values above 0.96 and root mean square error (RMSE) values below 1 m on the simulated training and testing datasets. Two independent simulation-based validations using benthic spectra excluded from model development yielded R2 values of 0.84 and 0.94, and RMSEs of 2.26 and 1.35 m, respectively. Median absolute percentage errors (MdAPEs) were below 15% across all simulated datasets. This model was applied to Sentinel-2/MSI imagery after OSW extraction, producing spatially coherent 10-m bathymetry maps across seven OSW regions. Independent validation using 13,296 ATL24 depths covering 20 reef sites yielded an R2 of 0.80, an RMSE of 0.75 m, and an MdAPE of 26.13%. Additional evaluations using airborne LiDAR and in situ SeaBASS observations, together with comparisons against two existing SDB models, demonstrated stable performance across geographically diverse OSWs. The model is designed for Case-1 OSWs shallower than 20 m, with better performance below 10 m, consistent with the depth range of benthic habitat mapping. OSW-SDB enables practical and transferable bathymetric mapping at 10-m resolution across diverse Case-1 OSWs using only Sentinel-2/MSI imagery, without requiring site-specific bathymetric or benthic priors during application.

title: Uncertainty-guided abundance reconstruction for robust hyperpansharpening
Advancing remote sensing of carbon fractions in coastal waters: retrieval algorithms and optical proxies for Sentinel-2 MSI and Sentinel-3 OLCI
abstract: A thorough understanding of the global carbon pools and cycle is essential for understanding and predicting the effects of climate change. Coastal waters play a key role in the global carbon cycle but remain poorly understood due to their optical complexity, high spatial variability, and sensitivity to climate change. Satellite remote sensing data can provide high spatial and temporal resolution for carbon monitoring at local, regional, and global scales. This study estimates the potential of Sentinel-2 MSI (S2) and Sentinel-3 OLCI (S3) for mapping carbon fractions in coastal waters. In situ hyperspectral reflectance measurements and concentrations of different carbon fractions, namely Total Organic Carbon (TOC), Dissolved Organic Carbon (DOC), Particulate Organic Carbon (POC), and Dissolved Inorganic Carbon (DIC), were used. Bio-optical and physical water parameters, as well as carbon fractions, were measured in the coastal areas of the eastern Baltic Sea from 2023 to 2024. In situ reflectance spectra were recalculated to S2 and S3 band reflectance using their respective spectral response functions. Regression models, including linear regression and machine learning methods, were developed and validated against in situ data to estimate carbon fractions. For S2, the combinations of green and red or red-edge bands achieved the best performance in carbon retrieval, with R 2 values of 0.67, 0.64, and 0.56 for TOC, DOC, and DIC, respectively. The corresponding MAPE values ranged from 14% to 18%, and biases were close to zero. Slightly higher accuracies were obtained with S3 simulations. The S3 models that used reflectance at 490, 620, and 665 nm produced the most accurate estimates for both TOC ( R 2 = 0.71) and DOC ( R 2 = 0.67). For DIC, the best predictive model combined information from 510, 665, and 709 nm bands, achieving R 2 of 0.62. Among the tested optical proxies, CDOM absorption at 443 nm showed the most consistent relationship with TOC, DOC, and DIC ( R 2 = 0.56–0.30). The study represents a significant step forward in the remote sensing of coastal waters, and if adopted, the proposed carbon-fraction products could enable substantial progress across various fields, from carbon-cycle research to monitoring and policymaking.

title: Tree crown mortality and defoliation assessment in temperate forests using aerial imagery and deep learning
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Forest health is increasingly threatened by global warming and recurrent droughts. However, limited long-term data on tree health and mortality restricts our ability to detect trends and predict forest responses to climate stressors. Traditional methods for assessing tree defoliation are accurate but costly and labor-intensive, highlighting the need for scalable alternatives. This study aims to develop a more automated approach for monitoring tree defoliation and mortality in Germany and Switzerland using deep learning applied to freely available aerial imagery.We assessed crown vitality using three and four defoliation classes derived from field surveys. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was trained on 48,388 annotated tree crowns from aerial imagery, labeled with forest type and defoliation status. RGB and NDVI-GB inputs were tested using five-fold and spatial-block cross-validation to ensure robustness.The three-class model outperformed the four-class CNN object detection version. RGB and NDVI-GB bands produced similar results in the three-class setup, with F1-scores of 0.74 and 0.73, respectively. Dead trees were detected with high accuracy (F1-score: 0.97), while healthy trees also showed good performance (F1-conifer: 0.78, F1-broadleaf: 0.73). Defoliated trees were more challenging to detect (F1-conifer: 0.61, F1-broadleaf: 0.54).This study demonstrates that RGB-based CNNs using three defoliation classes offer a scalable, automated solution for detecting tree mortality and quantifying defoliation at tree level. As more countries acquire repeated aerial imagery, this study offers broad applicability and supports forest inventories and resilient management strategies.

title: High spatial resolution Greenland Ice Sheet mass change linked to Greenland Blocking and North Atlantic Oscillation
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The low spatial resolution (300–400 km) of Gravity Recovery and Climate Experience (GRACE) and the 11-month data gap between GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) complicate the evaluation of long-term ice mass loss at sub-region scale. Although several studies have downscaled GRACE data for water storage evaluation, efforts to downscale ice mass change are limited. Here, we utilized multiscale geographically-weighted regression (MGWR) to improve the spatial resolution of GRACE-derived ice mass change from 0.25° to 5 km in Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS). The reconstructed results after downscaling demonstrate consistent temporal variation and reduced noise compared to other reconstruction methods for sub-regions and the entire GrIS. They can capture finer signals of ice mass change while maintaining original spatial characteristics. Validation against free air gravity anomalies changes also demonstrates the superior performance of the downscaled results over the reconstructed CSR Mascon data. For overlapping lines, the mean correlation coefficient (CC) increases from 0.13 to 0.32, with the mean root mean square error (RMSE) decreasing from 1.36 to 1.13. At the intersection points, the mean CC improves from 0.06 to 0.30, and the mean RMSE is reduced from 1.33 to 1.05. They are further used to detect the contributions of Greenland Blocking (GB) and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) to high-resolution ice mass change through precipitation and runoff in four sub-periods, during which the driving factors affecting ice mass change differ significantly. Additionally, NAO and GB can influence ice mass change through solid ice discharge by impacting surface temperature and sea-ice concentration.

title: High‑resolution L‑VOD mapping over China: A downscaling framework based on a differencing paradigm integrated with physical constraints (PhyDiF)
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Vegetation Optical Depth (VOD) is a key microwave-derived remote sensing parameter reflecting vegetation water content and supporting ecological and carbon-cycle studies. However, existing VOD products have coarse spatial resolution (∼9–36 km), limiting fine-scale applications. Statistical and machine-learning downscaling methods remain immature, lacking reliability and physical consistency, especially over large heterogeneous regions. To address this research gap, this study proposes the Physics-informed Differencing Downscaling Framework (PhyDiF). PhyDiF integrates a differencing paradigm with radiative transfer model (RTM)-based physical constraints. Rather than directly predicting absolute VOD values, the differencing paradigm predicts the differences in VOD ( Δ V O D ) induced by spatial resolution differences. The predicted Δ V O D is then combined with the coarse-resolution baseline VOD to reconstruct high-resolution absolute VOD. In addition, an RTM-based physical constraint is incorporated into a joint loss function to improve VOD prediction accuracy while promoting consistency between the predicted VOD and the corresponding brightness temperature (TB) simulated using the RTM. At the 9 km scale, direct validation of the differencing paradigm within PhyDiF and model selection among various baseline models show that U‑Net performs best in predicting Δ V O D , achieving a correlation coefficient with the true values of 0.854, with RMSE and MAE of only 0.016 and 0.011, respectively. Based on this, PhyDiF was constructed by incorporating physical constraints, generating a 3‑day 1 km PhyDiF VOD dataset over China from 2015 to 2021. Comprehensive evaluation shows that the PhyDiF VOD product outperforms the baseline product (MT‑DCA) and traditional interpolation results (Cubic) in spatial details, clearly depicting texture information and VOD spatial heterogeneity that more closely resemble actual land surface features. Correlations with above‑ground biomass (AGB), canopy height (CH), and leaf area index (LAI) are significantly improved compared with existing methods, both across China and in typical local areas. For example, in the low‑VOD area, compared with the Cubic method, the differencing‑paradigm‑based U‑Net and PhyDiF achieve improvements in correlation with AGB, CH, and LAI of 19.13 %/5.83 %/9.48 % and 32.17 %/10.42 %/17.43 %, respectively, while PhyDiF, incorporating physical constraints, outperforms U‑Net by 10.95 %, 4.33 %, and 7.26 %, respectively. In temporal validation, the product accurately exhibited the seasonal cycles and interannual dynamic trends of vegetation phenology, maintaining high consistency with MT‑DCA. Further scale consistency testing confirmed a correlation of 0.9997 with MT‑DCA and a standard deviation of only 0.007. Overall, PhyDiF provides a generalizable and reliable framework for generating high‑resolution VOD, advancing vegetation microwave remote sensing technology.

title: From pixel-level retrievals to bay-scale nutrient dynamics in Pärnu Bay using Sentinel-3 OLCI
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Monitoring nutrient dynamics is essential for assessing eutrophication in coastal waters, yet conventional in situ observations provide limited spatial coverage. This study evaluated the capability of Sentinel-3 Ocean and Land Colour Instrument (OLCI)-derived nutrient products to represent seasonal and interannual dynamics of total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) in Pärnu Bay, Gulf of Riga, during 2016–2024. Nutrient concentrations were estimated using regionally adapted OLCI retrieval algorithms and compared with in situ observations at pixel, seasonal, and annual scales. An additional comparison with operational Copernicus Marine Environment Monitoring Service (CMEMS) nutrient modelling products was carried out. Pixel-level validation yielded moderate agreement between OLCI-derived and in situ observations (TN: R 2 = 0.50, NRMSE = 26.5%; TP: R 2 = 0.33, NRMSE = 30.9%). Independent temporal validation using 2022–2024 observations retained comparable agreement (TN: R 2 = 0.44 and TP: R 2 = 0.47). However, spatial and temporal aggregation resulted in stronger overall correspondence and substantially lower error metrics. Seasonal TN products achieved an R 2 of 0.75 and NRMSE of 14.7%, while annual products reached an R 2 of 0.68 and NRMSE of 8.6%. Similar improvements were observed for TP, where annual aggregation increased R 2 to 0.54 and reduced NRMSE to 10.0%. The OLCI-derived products captured seasonal nutrient variability, interannual nutrient tendencies, and spatial nutrient gradients associated with riverine influence. These findings demonstrate that moderate pixel-level retrieval accuracy does not necessarily limit bay-scale monitoring capability. Spatially and temporally aggregated Sentinel-3 OLCI products provide a valuable complement to conventional monitoring programmes and show considerable potential for long-term eutrophication assessment in optically complex Baltic coastal waters.

title: Satellite observations reveal expanding high-latitude warming hotspots and regional contrasts on global surface temperature change
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Understanding the spatial and temporal variability of global surface warming is important for anticipating regional climate extremes and potential tipping points. However, conventional temperature indicators based on spatial averaging may obscure the evolution of persistent warming hotspots and the regional processes associated with surface temperature changes. Here, we analyze satellite-derived global land–ocean surface temperature (GLST) data from 2003 to 2023 and propose a three-dimensional (latitude-longitude-time) spatiotemporal clustering framework to characterize global warming patterns and identify persistent heat clusters. Globally, GLST increased at a rate of 0.025 ± 0.007 K/y, with land warming occurring 60% faster (0.034 ± 0.012 K/y) than over oceans (0.021 ± 0.006 K/y). Warming peaked prominently at ∼ 45°N (0.075 K/y in the Western Pacific; 0.066 K/y over Europe), primarily driven by dynamics in snow-climate zones and boreal forests. Spatiotemporal clustering revealed expanding heat anomalies in northern high latitudes (>45°N), where intensity (+0.027 K/y) and spatial coverage (+0.322 × 10⁶ km 2 /y) were positive; both metrics were larger in 2013–2023 than in 2003–2012, although the short-term trend is sensitive to individual extreme years. Notably, over land, non-radiative factors, including latent heat flux and soil moisture, were associated with regional differences in surface warming, with evaporative cooling effects reducing warming in several moisture-limited regions. These findings highlight the value of satellite observations and spatiotemporal clustering for identifying global warming hotspots and developing targeted adaptation strategies.

title: Assessing forest structural dynamics and post-disturbance early-stage recovery using PlanetScope imagery and photogrammetric point clouds
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Forests in the southeastern United States (US) are frequently disturbed by wind events, such as hurricanes, tornadoes, and severe windstorms, affecting ecosystem resilience, biodiversity, and carbon storage. Monitoring post-disturbance forest changes is challenging due to the limited availability of spatially continuous and temporally high-resolution canopy height data. To address these limitations, we evaluated the potential of PlanetScope data to assess forest structure and thematic changes across three wind-affected sites in the southeastern US: Oakmulgee (tornado), Flagg Mountain (straight-line wind), and Weeks Bay (hurricane). We used multi-stereo PlanetScope imagery to generate photogrammetric point clouds, which were processed to extract a suite of discrete canopy height metrics at different spatial resolutions (3 m, 10 m, 15 m, and 20 m) and validated using airborne lidar-derived canopy height metrics. Random Forest (RF) regression models were then developed using PlanetScope imagery, acquired concurrently with airborne lidar across study sites, and the trained models were applied to produce pre- and post-disturbance canopy height maps. Similarly, RF classification models were developed for three scenarios (airborne lidar acquisition date, pre-wind, and post-wind), and applied to generate forest/non-forest maps for pre- and post-disturbance periods, enabling assessment of thematic changes following wind disturbance. Results indicate that upper canopy height percentiles (95th and 98th) aggregated at a 20 m grid resolution produced the strongest agreement with airborne lidar measurements (correlation coefficient (r) = 0.32–0.33, Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) = 7.57–9.05 m). When the comparison was limited to grid cells where PlanetScope and lidar heights differed by 7 m or less, agreement improved (r = 0.68–0.79, RMSE = 3.70–4.35 m). RF canopy height estimation models showed moderate accuracy across study sites (R 2 = 0.51–0.54, RMSE = 2.45–4.31 m). Multi-temporal analysis using generated 20 m canopy height maps revealed substantial canopy height reductions after wind disturbance, affecting 40.47% of Oakmulgee site, 36.52% of Flagg Mountain, and 60.92% of Weeks Bay. Overall, the approach provides a promising framework for assessing and monitoring forest disturbance impacts. It captures post-disturbance changes in forest structure with an ability to provide spatially explicit and timely information on canopy structure and thematic dynamics, particularly in areas where airborne lidar or field measurements are limited.

title: Driver-specific temporal shifts in post-fire vegetation recovery: a multi-year Landsat-based analysis of the 2022 Uljin forest fire, South Korea
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: How the relative importance of environmental factors shifts during post-fire vegetation recovery remains underexplored in temperate forests with complex terrain and mixed-species canopies. This study examined the 2022 Uljin–Samcheok fire in South Korea (16,302 ha in total), focusing on the Uljin portion and integrating annual dNBR (differenced normalized burn ratio) multi-temporal data from Landsat 8/9 imagery for 2022–2025 with meteorological, topographic, and forest-structure variables at a 500 m grid scale, using the 892 grid cells in which dNBR ≥ 0.1 pixels covered at least 10% of the cell area. Annual ordinary least squares (OLS) models with a consistent structure enabled direct comparison of regression coefficients over time, providing a framework for evaluating temporal shifts in recovery correlates. Post-fire recovery dynamics were characterized not by a simple transition from terrain-dominated to meteorology-dominated controls, but by driver-specific temporal shifts. The positive association of slope with dNBR intensified through 2024 and then attenuated sharply in 2025, its standardized coefficient falling to roughly one-quarter of the 2024 peak (0.449 → 0.116), while northness maintained a persistent negative association throughout the recovery period. In contrast to Mediterranean studies, where topographic associations strengthen over time, this sharp attenuation of the slope constraint in the fourth year may be consistent with a recovery pathway in which temperate climatic conditions and the resprouting capacity of broadleaf forests weaken the persistence of topographic constraints. Antecedent seasonal meteorological associations diminished over time—from four significant variables in 2022 and seven in 2023 to three in 2024—and none remained significant in 2025, indicating that within the burned area the explanatory role of antecedent weather diminished as recovery progressed. This framework captures driver-specific shifts rarely addressed in existing studies and offers a reproducible approach applicable to other temperate forest fire sites.

title: From 2D toward 3D: City-scale artificial light at night distribution by super-resolution augmented spatiotemporal data modelling
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Artificial light at night (ALAN) distribution is crucial for a variety of studies, e.g., assessing spatially heterogeneous light pollution and resilient environments. Thus, new trends require mapping ALAN from a 2D plane toward complex 3D space. However, a robust method to estimate high-resolution ALAN distribution on 3D urban surfaces (including rooftop, façade, and ground) is still lacking. To tackle this challenge, we developed a super-resolution augmented spatiotemporal modelling framework with three hierarchical modules. First, SDGSAT-1 panchromatic and RGB imagery were fused to enhance multispectral ALAN information from 40-m to 10-m. Second, irradiance was redistributed to 1-m 3D point clouds using land use/land cover (LULC), building morphology, and an empirically supported vertical profile. Third, the estimates were evaluated using independent proxy observations from QMX-1 imagery and nighttime street-view imagery. Compared with a baseline 3D ALAN product generated directly from raw 10-m panchromatic irradiance, the proposed method increased the mean Spearman correlation coefficient from 0.498 to 0.625 across the four LULC types and three RGB bands, corresponding to a relative improvement of approximately 25.4%. The clearest gains occurred in commercial and industrial areas, whereas educational and residential areas showed weaker or non-significant improvements. The framework provides a scalable spatial redistribution approach for city-scale 3D ALAN representation, while remaining subject to uncertainties from simplified radiative assumptions, parameter transfer, and proxy validation data.

title: Online ecological-prior-guided bitemporal Transformer for mapping potential Spartina alterniflora eradication areas in coastal tidal flats
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Accurate monitoring of Spartina alterniflora eradication is essential for evaluating coastal wetland restoration and supporting invasive-species management. However, vegetation removal and natural surface variation can produce similar spectral changes in heterogeneous tidal flats, complicating image-based detection. To address this issue, we propose COAST ( Coastal Online Adaptive Spatiotemporal Transformer ), an online ecological-prior-guided bitemporal Transformer for mapping potential S. alterniflora eradication areas in the Jiangsu coastal tidal flats, China. The framework uses geographically weighted discriminant analysis (GWDA) posterior probabilities to represent spatially heterogeneous relationships between S. alterniflora pre-eradication spectral features and removal-related change. These probabilities provide soft supervision for a lightweight online prior encoder, whose output modulates bitemporal features through spatial prior gating. Training uses spatial-block out-of-fold GWDA predictions, and inference uses paired images with the prior generated from the pre-eradication image. Under a spatially separated evaluation design, COAST achieved the highest mean F1-score (95.00 %) and IoU (90.48 %) among the evaluated baselines across three random-seed runs. It also achieved a boundary F1-score of 81.25 %, a 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 256.04 m, and a changed-area fraction mean absolute error of 0.82 percentage points. Ablation experiments supported the contribution of prior-guided learning relative to the BiT backbone. Evaluation on manually annotated cross-year patches yielded F1-scores of 88.27 % for 2020–2023 and 93.13 % for 2020–2025, supporting temporal transfer within the sampled coastal settings. Local errors included agricultural-background false positives and incomplete target recovery. COAST provides an image-based workflow for repeated regional screening of eradication-related change and the prioritisation of follow-up verification.

title: Assessing Dothistroma needle blight severity in Pinus radiata using UAV multispectral imagery
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Dothistroma needle blight (DNB) is a major foliar disease of Pinus radiata , an important plantation species in several Southern Hemisphere countries. DNB management and resistance breeding depend on subjective, labour-intensive visual severity scoring that is difficult to scale. Prior UAV studies have used broad severity categories and crown-mean reflectance, discarding both the ordinal structure of the field grade and the within-crown spatial pattern of infection. This study evaluated whether UAV multispectral imagery can quantify tree-scale DNB severity while preserving the ordinal 5 % field grading, treating adjacent-class errors as less severe than distant ones. From imagery of two trials in the North Island, New Zealand, 8,136 manually delineated crowns were characterised by 552 candidate features (82 vegetation indices and 10 raw bands, each summarised by six within-crown distributional statistics). After collinearity filtering, 40 features were used to fit Ordinal Forest (OF) and Frequency-Adjusted Borders Ordinal Forest (fabOF) models at three granularities (5, 10, and 19 severity classes). At 19-class resolution, predictions fell within ± 10 points of the true severity for approximately 80 % of crowns. Quadratic weighted kappa rose with granularity, consistent with finer models erring predominantly by small, adjacent-class amounts. fabOF improved ordinal ranking, with markedly less underestimation between 50 and 70 % severity, whereas OF was sharper in the well-sampled moderate range, a calibration-balance trade-off across applications. Within-crown variability and tail-percentile statistics, not crown-mean reflectance, carried the strongest signal (SHAP analysis), consistent with DNB’s patchy progression. UAV multispectral imagery can therefore support fine-grained DNB severity assessment, an automated complement to visual scoring for management and resistance phenotyping, demonstrated here across two juvenile trials.

title: Improving urban green space quality for low‑carbon access in the 15‑minute city: an Access‑to‑Abatement framework
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Urban green-space (UGS) distribution and quality shape residents’ destination choices, travel behaviour and associated carbon emissions, yet few studies connect spatial accessibility and group-specific travel responses to carbon outcomes. We developed an integrated Access-to-Abatement (A2A) framework to assess whether targeted UGS quality upgrades can reduce reliance on destinations beyond the 15-minute catchment and lower travel-related emissions. A2A integrates a floating catchment area-based accessibility model with probabilistic destination allocation, UGS supply and quality, survey-informed group-specific preferences and travel-emission accounting. It quantifies accessibility gains and emission-reduction potential while tracing how local provision deficits and quality upgrades reallocate modelled visits. For communities below the citywide mean in either 15-minute accessibility or the mean quality of UGSs reachable within 15 min, we expanded destination sets using group- and mode-specific maximum acceptable travel times. This conditional expansion increased modelled accessibility but also reliance on motorised travel and associated emissions. Targeted upgrades within the 15-minute catchment mitigated this trade-off by reallocating modelled visits towards local UGSs, thereby improving 15-minute accessibility and reducing travel-related emissions. The emission-reduction effects were spatially uneven: peri -urban upgrades produced the largest local reductions, whereas central upgrades produced larger citywide reductions through demand reallocation. Abatement also followed a distance-dependent pattern, with the strongest reductions near upgraded UGSs, a rebound at intermediate distances and attenuation farther away. The framework identifies where quality upgrades can improve 15-minute accessibility and reduce travel emissions, supporting site-specific interventions based on UGS’s baseline deficiencies.

abstract: To meet the growing need for timely, frequent, and consistent long-term land surface information, the Annual NLCD Collection 1.0 integrates methodologies from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) and the Land Change Monitoring, Assessment, and Projection (LCMAP) initiative with modern geospatial deep-learning approaches. The resulting product suite provides six annual 30-m products for the conterminous United States (CONUS) spanning 1985–2023: Land Cover, Land Cover Change, Land Cover Confidence, Fractional Impervious Surface, Impervious Descriptor, and Spectral Change Day of Year. The overall accuracy of the NLCD 16-class thematic land cover product was 64.7 ± 0.5% across the study period and increased to 76.9 ± 0.4% when agreement included a match with either the primary or alternate reference label. Overall accuracy remained stable over time ranging from 64.5% to 65.0%. Even with increased temporal resolution, Annual NLCD maintained comparable accuracy to that of previous NLCD products mapped at 2–3-year intervals. Change detection accuracy for Annual NLCD was low, consistent with the difficulty of detecting and dating annual land cover transitions. User's and producer's accuracies varied considerably across change themes. Water gain and loss, forest loss, and shrubland gain were the better-detected change types, while most other change themes had accuracy <40% when allowing a ± 2-year buffer to define agreement. Despite its finer thematic classification scheme, the Annual NLCD product substantially improved change accuracy relative to LCMAP. Based on the Annual NLCD maps, approximately 19.4% of CONUS experienced at least one land cover change during 1985–2023. Annual NLCD products provide a consistent annual record of land cover and land use information to support diverse downstream applications.

title: Dem-assisted visual geolocation integrating ephemeris-based orientation correction with Multi-Scale skyline features
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Accurate geolocation in GNSS-denied mountainous environments remains a significant challenge for navigation and field operations. While vision-based methods using terrain features like skylines offer a promising passive solution, their performance is often hindered by unknown camera orientation, low feature discriminability across vast areas, and severe degradation under nighttime conditions. To address these limitations, this paper presents a novel visual geolocation framework that synergistically couples ephemeris-based orientation correction with multi-scale skyline feature matching. First, an Edge-Enhanced SegFormer-B3 (EESFormer-B3) network is developed for robust skyline extraction from query images, where a lightweight Edge Gate mechanism is integrated to refine boundary precision, particularly under low-light scenarios. Second, we propose a camera heading estimation method utilizing solar and lunar ephemeris, eliminating reliance on external heading sensors and drastically reducing the matching search space. Third, for matching, a hierarchical composite feature is designed, encoding the skyline's global shape trends, local directional variations, and dominant structural distributions to ensure robustness against repetitive terrain patterns. Extensive experiments were conducted in a complex 700 km² mountainous region. The results demonstrate that our method achieves a localization success rate of 82% (daytime) and 76% (nighttime) within a 250-meter error threshold. The ephemeris-based correction alone accelerates the matching process by over 30 times compared to an unconstrained orientation search. This work provides a reliable, efficient, and illumination-invariant geolocation solution, with strong potential for applications in autonomous navigation, search and rescue, and other field missions in GNSS-compromised natural environments.

title: The Bovine Slurry Index (BSI): An integrated framework for manure pond mapping using GeoFM-derived cattle-operation detection and Sentinel-2 spectral formulation
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Quantifying greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from livestock operations is a prerequisite for reconciling bottom-up inventories with atmospheric observations. However, global GHG reporting remains limited by a lack of spatially explicit data on animal waste management systems (AWMS), forcing reliance on coarse regional assumptions rather than operation-level observations. Existing geospatial foundation models partly address this spatial gap by mapping cattle-operation footprints that provide upstream spatial context, but contextual detection alone cannot identify the manure-management features within them. To address this gap, we introduce the Bovine Slurry Index (BSI), an empirical Sentinel-2 spectral index for detecting liquid/slurry manure ponds within known cattle-operation footprints. The primary formulation, BSI-E, uses calibrated narrow-NIR (B8A) and SWIR-1 (B11) reflectance bounds derived from manure pond samples in the United States and China. The index targets the empirically observed intermediate NIR-SWIR response of manure ponds relative to clear water, vegetation, dry holding pens, and exposed soil. Calibration used 2,730 pond samples from the U.S. and China, and segmentation was evaluated against 945 reference polygons across all five geographic regions. BSI-E produced stronger pond-to-background contrast and higher segmentation accuracy than evaluated water indices, with dataset-level intersection-over-union (IoU) ranging from 0.26 in Brazil to 0.68 in the United States and precision reaching 0.91. Optimal thresholds varied geographically from 0.25 to 1.00, and performance was strongest in dryland feedlot systems and lower in humid or spectrally mixed settings. BSI provides a target-specific spectral method for generating operation-scale evidence that could inform AWMS activity data within these footprints.

title: Physics-constrained spatio-temporal generative adversarial learning for daily-scale sea ice thickness prediction
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: With the rapid shrinkage of Arctic sea ice, predicting its spatio-temporal changes has become an important technical basis for studies of polar climate. Existing physics-driven and data-driven paradigms show respective advantages in representing sea-ice process mechanisms and learning complex spatio-temporal patterns; however, both remain challenged in balancing prediction accuracy with physics consistency. Therefore, this study proposes a daily-scale spatio-temporal sea ice thickness (SIT) prediction method driven by both data and physics, namely the Physics-Constrained Generative Adversarial Network (PCGAN). To incorporate sea-ice physics principles into the data-driven prediction process, PCGAN is designed at three levels: the generator, the discriminators, and physics-rule constraints. First, a Physics-Augmented Cross-Process Interaction (PA-CPI) module is designed in the generator to enhance the ability of the model to represent the physically coupled mechanisms among multiple geophysics variables, including sea ice, snow, wind fields, and temperature. Second, a spatio-temporal dual-discriminator architecture is proposed to jointly constrain the local spatial structures and temporal increments of SIT. Finally, the freezing-degree-day growth relationship and the daily-scale thickness change-rate relationship are transformed into bounded physics consistency scores and embedded into temporal adversarial learning to improve the physics plausibility of the generator-predicted results. Experimental results in the Arctic Ocean during the cold season show that PCGAN maintains stable performance under different random initializations. Its average RMSE is 0.1035 m, which is 12.73% lower than that of MSS-STFormer, the best-performing baseline model. Physics-related statistical metrics, such as the anomalous thinning rate, also show that the predictions of PCGAN are closer to the observed statistical characteristics than those of the other deep learning models. Multidimensional spatio-temporal analyses further confirm the stable predictive performance of PCGAN under different prediction conditions. The interpretability analysis shows that the model’s responses to multiple geophysical factors are broadly consistent with established physical understanding of sea-ice evolution. Ablation experiments and threshold-sensitivity analyses verify the effectiveness of the key model structures and the physics consistency constraints. PCGAN demonstrates the potential of incorporating physics consistency constraints into data-driven frameworks to improve SIT prediction accuracy and physical plausibility, providing methodological support for Arctic SIT prediction during the cold season.

Road space as memory and inference: A unified geometry-centric framework for trajectory forecasting
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: High-definition (HD) vector maps are essential to trajectory forecasting, yet existing methods often use them only as passive context and remain dependent on identity-consistent tracking histories. We propose a unified geometry-centric forecasting framework that treats road-space geometry as an active computational substrate for both future prediction and history recovery under tracking-available and no-tracking conditions. The framework uses a common road-space representation and topology-guided decoupled decoder architecture across both settings, while differing only in how motion history is constructed. With reliable tracking, agent history is incrementally aggregated across shifting local frames for efficient streaming inference. Without tracking, frame-wise detections are projected into lane-space occupancy memories, from which target-specific history is recovered through geometry-conditioned querying. The decoder then generates topology-consistent motion intents and realizes them as final trajectories using surrounding-agent interactions. Experiments on Argoverse 2 (AV2), Argoverse 1 (AV1), and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset (WOMD) show that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance under reliable tracking and supports low-latency streaming inference, reaching 44.32 ms per frame with pre-encoded maps. Under no-tracking conditions, the occupancy-based pathway preserves most of the tracking-available performance on the primary K = 6 metrics, with relative increases in minFDE 6 , minADE 6 , and MR 6 limited to 6%–8% on AV2 and below 3% on AV1 and WOMD. Additional validation on real sensor data with annotated detections and a tracking-by-detection association pipeline shows that the occupancy-based pathway remains robust to tracking identity errors, whereas identity-dependent methods degrade substantially. These results demonstrate that actively exploiting road-space geometry can substantially reduce trajectory forecasting’s reliance on upstream tracking.

title: Mapping the spatial extent of agroforestry lands across Africa by characterizing tree spatial arrangements
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Agroforestry is a land-use practice that integrates trees into agricultural lands, supporting food security and rural livelihoods while delivering both climate adaptation and mitigation benefits. However, current large-scale assessments often rely on coarse tree canopy cover or biomass products to approximate agroforestry, which results in biases estimates of the production and ecological effects from agroforestry. Here, we produced a 100 m resolution map of the spatial extent of agroforestry lands in Africa for 2019, using 10 m resolution tree canopy cover data derived from PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 imagery. This map explicitly delineates croplands where agroforestry system is practised by distinguishing tree spatial patterns within croplands, focusing on irregularly scattered trees and trees aligned in rows. Scattered trees are identified using tree-pixel distance metrics, whereas trees planted in rows are detected using a U-Net model trained with ~38,000 manually labelled tree-row features. The identified agroforestry lands with scattered trees and trees in rows on cropland were validated against ground-based sites collected from the literature and Google Earth imagery, yielding an overall accuracy of 77.2%. This agroforestry dataset with explicit spatial tree arrangements can served as a baseline for assessing environmental impacts and crop yield change of agroforestry ecosystems, as well as for supporting the development of process-based agroforestry models.

title: Geospatial assessment of seaweed cultivation suitability using ocean color data and multi-criteria decision analysis in the coastal waters of Lombok Island, Indonesia
abstract: The rapid expansion of Kappaphycus alvarezii cultivation in Indonesia poses significant sustainability challenges due to ad hoc site selection, which has contributed to disease outbreaks and exceeded ecological carrying capacities. This study employs ocean color remote sensing and Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) to develop a knowledge-driven geospatial model for identifying suitable habitat zones on Lombok Island. By integrating the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) and Weighted Linear Combination (WLC), a biophysical hierarchy is established that prioritizes physiological survival over theoretical yield maximization. To enhance model robustness in the absence of independent yield data, a Map Removal Sensitivity Analysis (MRSA) was implemented to quantify the relative influence and spatial sensitivity of key environmental parameters. The results indicate sea surface temperature (21.46%) and salinity (15.33%) as the most influential variables, supporting a “survival-first” paradigm for mitigating ice-ice disease risks. The geospatial analysis reveals a spatial pattern of high suitability consistent with an “environmentally balanced” zone, characterized by depths of approximately 2–30 m and current velocities of 0.2–0.4 m/s. Sensitivity results further show that while SST exerts a dominant but spatially uniform control, salinity and dissolved oxygen drive localized variability, identifying regional-scale sensitivity gradients whose ecological interpretation is bounded by the resolution of the underlying data. Quantitative spatial validation against 275 georeferenced farm GPS locations shows that 96.7% of farms are concentrated in the southern high-suitability zone, against an area-based null expectation of 26.0% for that cluster (chi-square = 716.7, df = 2, p < 0.001). A per-suitability-class overlay further confirms that 98.9% of farms fall within High-suitability pixels and none within Low-suitability pixels against an area-based null of 66.9% (chi-square p < 0.001); Cohen’s κ against a random background is modest (0.08), reflecting the abundance of high-suitability habitat relative to the small number of realized farms. These findings provide a practical and transferable framework for supporting Allocated Zones for Aquaculture (AZAs) and identifying growing-season and risk-informed aquaculture sites in data-limited coastal regions. The resulting model constitutes a growing-season suitability index explicitly framed for the East Monsoon cultivation window (June–August), and provides a spatially explicit, satellite-informed decision-support tool for K. alvarezii site selection in Lombok Island waters.

title: First results of joint sea surface salinity, temperature, and wind speed retrieval from MICAP Simultaneous L/C/K-band active and passive observations
abstract: The Microwave Imager Combined Active and Passive (MICAP) onboard the Chinese Ocean Salinity Satellite (HY-4A) is a novel spaceborne payload developed for the simultaneous retrieval of Sea Surface Salinity (SSS), Sea Surface Temperature (SST), and Sea Surface Wind Speed (WS). MICAP uniquely combines L-band (1.4 GHz), C-band (6.9 GHz), and K-band (18.7 GHz) one-dimensional (1-D) interferometric synthetic aperture radiometers with an L-band Digital Beam-Forming (DBF) scatterometer. This paper presents the Level-2 retrieval algorithms and preliminary validation results obtained during the early in-orbit verification phase of the MICAP ocean products. The retrieval framework adopts a two-step strategy, including an L-band only SSS retrieval scheme (Mode-1) and a combined multi-parameter retrieval scheme (Mode-2). In Mode-2, the simultaneous C/K-band measurements are first used to derive estimates of SST and WS. These auxiliary parameters are subsequently combined with the L-band radiometer and scatterometer measurements to perform the final SSS and WS retrieval. Preliminary validation against Argo observations shows an SSS RMSE of approximately 0.58 psu for the Mode-2 retrieval over the screened open ocean validation sample. The retrieved SST and WS products show RMSEs of 0.80 K and 1.17 m/s, respectively, when compared with iQuam and TAO buoy data. These results provide an initial in-orbit demonstration of simultaneous multi-parameter retrieval using the MICAP multi-frequency active and passive observations.

title: Performance Evaluation of Embedded AI Inference on Zynq Ultrascale+ and Versal SoCs for Onboard Space Applications
Flexible Focus Sampling for Depth from Focus
FLORO: A multimodal geospatial foundation model for ecological remote sensing across sensors and scales
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: The proliferation of remote sensing platforms has generated an unprecedented diversity of Earth observation data, creating both the opportunity and the challenge of extracting transferable knowledge across sensors, scales, and environments. Foundation models have emerged as a promising framework for this challenge, leveraging large datasets to learn representations that generalize across tasks and sensing conditions in real-world Earth observation. However, many current approaches rely on very large pretraining datasets and remain constrained by fixed sensor configurations, limited observation-type flexibility, or narrow evaluation settings. These limitations are particularly relevant for ecological and environmental applications, where data are often heterogeneous across platforms, resolutions, and data sources. We introduce FLORO, a multimodal geospatial foundation model designed to learn transferable representations from a comparatively small, heterogeneous remote-sensing pretraining dataset. FLORO is pretrained using masked autoencoding on a heterogeneous combination of Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, SkySAT imagery, terrain data, and UAV-derived products. To accommodate real-world sensor variability, FLORO incorporates availability-aware inputs that indicate which spectral bands and auxiliary observations are present in each sample, enabling a unified input space across heterogeneous sensor configurations. We evaluated FLORO on the PANGAEA benchmark under a frozen-encoder protocol across scene classification, segmentation, and regression tasks. Despite being pretrained on a smaller dataset than competing foundation models, FLORO achieved strong and stable transfer across optical, optical-SAR, and optical-elevation benchmarks spanning medium-resolution satellite, airborne, and ultra-high-resolution UAV imagery. FLORO obtained the second-best average segmentation performance across six PANGAEA benchmarks, the third-best average rank across three scene-classification benchmarks, and excelled in regression tasks, while qualitative results showed improved preservation of spatial structure in flood, urban, biomass, and canopy-height prediction settings. Overall, these results position FLORO as a practical framework for ecological and environmental monitoring under heterogeneous sensing conditions. To support benchmarking and reproducibility, the source code and PANGAEA evaluation integration, including access to the benchmark datasets, are available at https://github.com/jorlrodriguezg/floro , with pretrained model checkpoints at https://huggingface.co/jorlrodriguezg/floro .

title: A retrieval method for passive microwave LST integrating radiative transfer-informed land-air environmental conditions
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Passive microwave (PMW) remote sensing is a significant data source for generating spatiotemporally continuous land surface temperature (LST). Although empirical methods can retrieve PMW LST that approximates the physical meaning of thermal infrared (TIR)-derived LST, they generally fail to fully consider land-air variables implied by PMW radiative transfer principles. Particularly, the impacts of atmospheric situation have often been overlooked. Here, we propose a machine learning-based retrieval method that integrates a broader range of land-air environmental variables in accordance with PMW radiative transfer principles (PLST-ILA). Validation against pre-extracted MODIS LST shows that the proposed method achieves annual daytime and nighttime root mean square errors (RMSEs) of 3.17 K and 2.21 K, respectively, showing reductions of 9.9 %∼26.1 % relative to the five reference methods. Validation at six in-situ sites indicates that PLST-ILA yields an annual daytime RMSE of 4.21 K and a nighttime RMSE of 4.02 K, reducing the daytime RMSE by 0.33 ∼ 1.68 K and the nighttime RMSE by 0.27 ∼ 1.32 K benchmarked by four advanced methods. The monthly-scale model generally achieves superior performance compared with the seasonal-scale and annual-scale models. Moreover, accounting for topographic and geomorphological characteristics, anthropogenic emissions, atmospheric humidity, and aerosol optical depth may further improve retrieval accuracy. Finally, the proposed method demonstrates the capability to reconstruct PMW observations within orbital gaps. Validation against gap-retained MODIS LST yields annual RMSEs of 3.68 K during the daytime and 2.69 K at night. The results of this study provide a technical reference for PMW LST retrieval and may contribute to optimizing the precision of thermal-related research.

title: Remote sensing of lake surface water temperature reveals divergent hydroclimatic associations with lake ice phenology across China
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Lake ice phenology is a sensitive indicator of climate change, yet its regional hydroclimatic associations remain poorly understood. Here, we reconstructed daily lake surface water temperature (LSWT) from MODIS for 583 lakes across China and derived freeze-up date (FUD), break-up date (BUD), and ice cover duration (ICD) for 376 seasonally ice-covered lakes. Robustness was evaluated with sensitivity tests, meteorological observations, transition-period comparisons, and passive-microwave ice records; Mann-Kendall tests, Theil-Sen slopes, VIF-constrained XGBoost-SHAP, and structural equation modeling assessed trends and regional associations. FUD was delayed in all three ice-covered regions, whereas BUD was delayed in the Tibetan Plateau Lake Region (TPR) but advanced in the Mongolian-Xinjiang Lake Region (MXR) and Northeast Lake Region (NLR), resulting in shorter ICD in all regions. Regional mean ICD declined by 0.03, 0.35, and 0.47 d yr -1 in the TPR, MXR, and NLR, respectively; significant lake-level changes were concentrated in the TPR, with 72 and 33 lakes showing significant FUD and BUD trends. All nine models retained positive hold-out R 2 (0.535–0.960). SHAP attributions differed by region: radiative variables dominated in the TPR, the MXR showed metric-specific associations with wind, snowfall, geographic, and thermal , and geographic, radiative, and morphometric variables dominated in the NLR. Structural equation models indicated stronger precipitation-related associations in the NLR and snowfall-related associations in the MXR and TPR. These results reveal pronounced regional heterogeneity in lake ice responses to warming and the value of integrating remote sensing, interpretable machine learning, and pathway modeling to resolve these contrasts.

title: Score-space knowledge graph propagation for generalized multi-label zero-shot classification of remote sensing images
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Generalized multi-label zero-shot learning predicts seen and unseen labels from a predefined vocabulary, yet independent image-text matching leaves label relations unused. We propose Score-TEGAR, which refines frozen GeoRSCLIP scores through a typed label-relation graph. Seen-label statistics define co-occurrence, exclusion, and hierarchy; text affinity connects unseen labels. The Typed-Edge Graph Attention Refiner (TEGAR) combines relation-specific propagation, a non-positive exclusion residual, and uncertainty-aware scaling. Across MLRSNet, BigEarthNet, and China-MAS-50k, it achieved the highest mean harmonic mean of seen and unseen mean average precision (mAP-HM) among thirteen configurations: 0.614, 0.439, and 0.476. Parameter-matched controls support the contribution of typed graph structure, while label-level analysis reveals uneven benefits across unseen categories. Score-space refinement provides a route to structured prediction when candidate labels are known but training annotations are incomplete.

title: Towards fractional vegetation cover mapping in complex mountain environments through a knowledge-guided unmixing framework
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Mountain vegetation dynamics serve as sensitive indicators of environmental change, making accurate fractional cover mapping of primary components crucial for understanding ecosystem responses. This task has been facilitated by multispectral satellite imagery, particularly Sentinel-2, which provides continuous observations. To translate these observations into fractional cover maps, existing studies typically apply fraction estimation models to synthetic spectra derived from field-measured signatures. However, limited field surveys in mountain terrain present a data bottleneck for synthetic spectra construction, while complex vegetation composition introduces spectral ambiguities that existing methods struggle to represent. Therefore, this study develops a knowledge-guided unmixing framework for annual mapping of the fractional cover of herbaceous vegetation, woody vegetation, and bare land in mountain environments using Sentinel-2 time series. Specifically, to overcome data bottleneck, we develop a knowledge-guided strategy that automatically builds adaptive physio-phenological feature spaces to extract representative signatures. To resolve spectral ambiguity, we incorporate nonlinear mixing mechanisms to synthesize spectra that better represent complex mixing relationships. The synthetic library was then used to train Unmix-Net, a spectral-temporal regression model for fraction estimation. The framework was applied to the central Qilian Mountains and southern Hengduan Mountains spanning broad climatic gradients, validated with high-resolution UAV data. It achieved MAEs of 12.38 %, 8.58 %, and 9.82 % for herbaceous, woody, and bare land, outperforming existing models by up to 7.80 %. When implemented across landscapes ranging from arid steppes and alpine meadows to tropical rainforests, the framework maintained comparable performance. The comparative experiments further confirmed that the proposed extraction strategy improved the balance of component estimates, while combining complementary mixing mechanisms reduced estimation errors. By integrating domain knowledge into data-driven learning, this framework supports spatially continuous fractional vegetation mapping in mountain environments.
